facts.title: Named After a Pink Rose
facts.text: Rhodium was discovered in 1803 by the English chemist William Hyde Wollaston while studying crude platinum ore from South America. He named it from the Greek word 'rhodon', meaning rose, because the salts he extracted formed beautiful rose-red solutions. The same batch of ore also led Wollaston to discover palladium the year before.

facts.title: Rarest of the Precious Metals
facts.text: Rhodium is one of the scarcest elements in Earth's crust, with an abundance of only about 0.0002 parts per million, far rarer than gold or platinum. It is almost never found on its own and instead occurs mixed into platinum and nickel ores. The bulk of the world's supply comes from the Bushveld Igneous Complex in South Africa.

facts.title: The Catalytic Converter King
facts.text: Roughly 80 percent of all rhodium produced goes into catalytic converters in cars and trucks. There it performs a job few other metals can match: it converts toxic nitrogen oxides from engine exhaust back into harmless nitrogen and oxygen gas. This single application makes rhodium critical to clean-air regulations worldwide.

facts.title: Briefly More Valuable Than Gold
facts.text: Because it is so rare and industrially essential, rhodium's price can swing wildly. In early 2021 it spiked to around 29,000 US dollars per troy ounce, making it more than ten times the price of gold at the time. These dramatic prices are driven almost entirely by demand from the automotive industry.

facts.title: A Mirror That Never Tarnishes
facts.text: Rhodium is prized for its brilliant, highly reflective silver-white surface and its extreme resistance to corrosion and tarnish. It does not react with air, water, or most acids even at high temperatures. For this reason, jewelers electroplate white gold and silver with a thin layer of rhodium to give pieces a durable, dazzling shine.

facts.title: A Stubbornly Inert Metal
facts.text: Rhodium is remarkably unreactive: it resists attack by most acids and is not dissolved even by aqua regia, the potent mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acid that dissolves gold and platinum. Only hot concentrated sulfuric acid or molten alkali salts will slowly corrode it. This chemical toughness is part of why it lasts so long as a coating and catalyst.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Like other heavy elements, rhodium is not made on Earth but in the cosmos through processes inside stars. Astronomers believe much of it forms in the violent neutron-capture reactions of supernova explosions and merging neutron stars. The atoms in any piece of rhodium jewelry were created billions of years ago in stellar catastrophes.

facts.title: Just One Stable Isotope
facts.text: Natural rhodium consists entirely of a single stable isotope, rhodium-103, making it a 'monoisotopic' element. Only a handful of elements share this trait of having just one naturally occurring isotope. All of rhodium's other isotopes are radioactive and have very short half-lives.

facts.title: A Record-Setting Award
facts.text: Rhodium is so valuable that it has been used to honor exceptional achievements. Guinness World Records once presented Paul McCartney with a rhodium-plated disc to mark his status as the best-selling songwriter and recording artist. Its rarity made it a fitting symbol for surpassing even platinum-level records.

facts.title: No Known Role in Life
facts.text: Rhodium has no known biological function in any living organism, and humans encounter it only in tiny amounts. Its compounds are generally considered to have low toxicity because the metal is so chemically inert and rarely enters the body. Some rhodium complexes are nonetheless studied in laboratories as potential anticancer agents and as catalysts for making pharmaceuticals.
